# Genesis 15 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Genesis 15 consists of two divine encounters: vv. 1–6 (at night, in a vision, concerning the promised seed) and vv. 7–21 (at sundown, partly in a deep sleep, concerning the promised land). It records the formal inauguration of the Abrahamic covenant.

— Bruce Waltke, cited at preceptaustin.org/genesis-15-commentary

Ray Pritchard calls it "one of the most important chapters in all the Bible" because here we find the details of the Abrahamic covenant, which Paul and other NT writers treat as the foundation of the Christian gospel.
— preceptaustin.org/genesis-15-commentary

---

## v. 1 — "After these events, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: 'Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.'"

**Traditional / Evangelical reading:**

"After these things" refers to the war with the four kings, the rescue of Lot, and Abram's refusal of spoil from the king of Sodom (ch. 14). Abram had reason to fear reprisal from the defeated kings, and he had just sacrificed earthly reward. God addresses both needs: "shield" = protection; "reward" = recompense for what Abram gave up.

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/
— preceptaustin.org/genesis-15-commentary

This is the first occurrence of the phrase "the word of the LORD came" in Scripture (used over 100 times thereafter). It is also the first time God says "fear not" to anyone, and the first time God is called a "shield." The phrase "the word of the LORD came" introduces revelation to a prophet; Abram is explicitly called a prophet in Genesis 20:7.

— preceptaustin.org/genesis-15-commentary

Gill identifies "the word of the LORD" as Christ, the essential Word, appearing in human form.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/15.htm

Ellicott notes the revelation is made at night, not in a dream but in a trance (v. 5 mentions going outside to see stars). The patriarch needed more formal assurances — of offspring and land — after years of waiting.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

Matthew Henry suggests God came lest Abram be too "elevated and pleased" with his military victory and the meeting with Melchizedek; God had "better things in store."

— Cited at preceptaustin.org/genesis-15-commentary

Spurgeon is quoted: "I do not think that any human mind can ever grasp the fullness of meaning of these four words, 'I am thy reward.' God himself the reward of his faithful people."

— Cited at enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

---

## vv. 2–3 — Abram's reply: "O Lord GOD, what can You give me, since I remain childless…"

**Traditional reading:**

Abram's question is not rebellious doubt but honest frustration brought before God. It is "a doubt that desires God's promise" rather than one that denies it. Abram essentially says: "What good is reward if I have no son to inherit it? Where are the descendants You promised?"

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Gill adds that Abram saw beyond temporal blessings — he was concerned about the promised Messiah who would come through his line.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/15.htm

Ellicott notes a "slight tone of complaint": no reward can be truly great without an heir. He also explains the rare Hebrew phrase *ben-meshek* ("son of possession" = heir) and the wordplay with *Dammesek* (Damascus).

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

On "one born in my house" (v. 3), Ellicott clarifies that the Hebrew means "the son of my house" — the chief servant next to Abram, not a biological son. He was "not born of me, but the chief of the house."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

---

## vv. 4–5 — God's promise: "This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir… count the stars… So shall your offspring be."

**Traditional reading:**

God clarifies: the heir will be a biological son, not Eliezer. Then God takes Abram outside and uses the stars as an illustration of the countless number of descendants. Though the promise is repeated with clarity, its fulfilment (Isaac's birth) was still about 15 years away (Abram was ~85; Isaac born when he was 100). This illustrates that believers need both "faith and patience to inherit the promises" (Hebrews 6:11–12).

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Gill notes that Abram was famous in antiquity for astronomy/astrology, yet even he could not number the stars — the promise is of an innumerable seed, both natural (Hebrews 11:12) and spiritual (those of the same faith).

— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/15.htm

Ellicott observes that the stars visible to the naked eye are not vastly numerous, but they have always been "a received metaphor for an infinite multitude" because as one gazes, ever-fainter constellations appear.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

The greatest descendant is the "Bright and Morning Star" — Christ (Revelation 22:16).

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

---

## v. 6 — "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness."

This is arguably the most theologically freighted verse in Genesis. Here is where the major Protestant traditions converge and where some differences emerge.

### Traditional / Evangelical (broadly shared):

This is the first use of both "believe" (*aman*) and "righteousness" (*tsedaqah*) in Scripture. It is quoted four times in the NT (Romans 4:3, 4:9–10, 4:19–24; Galatians 3:5–7). It is the clearest OT expression of salvation by grace through faith. There are two kinds of righteousness: accomplished by human effort (impossible) and accounted by God's decree (through faith). God credits a real righteousness — Christ's — not a pretended one.

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Gill stresses it is not the act of believing itself that is the righteousness, but the object of faith — Christ and His righteousness — that is imputed. Abram was justified while still uncircumcised (Romans 4:9–10 makes much of this), so it cannot be by works or ritual.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/15.htm

Ellicott: "We have here the germ of the doctrine of free justification." Abram was a holy man who proved his faith by works, yet the inspired narrator places this declaration here — not after the offering of Isaac — "where all that Abram did was to believe, and for that belief's sake was accounted righteous before God."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

### Reformed / Baptist (John Piper / Desiring God):

Piper teaches that "faith is credited as righteousness" does **not** mean that our faith itself is our righteousness. Rather, faith unites us to Christ, and in union with Christ, God's righteousness (an "alien righteousness") is credited to us. Faith is the instrument, not the ground, of justification. Piper stresses 2 Corinthians 5:21 (double imputation: our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us) and argues that "faith connects you to God's righteousness."

— desiringgod.org/messages/faith-and-the-imputation-of-righteousness

Piper also distinguishes between the initial act of justifying faith (Genesis 15) and persevering faith (Genesis 17, at least 13 years later). Justification is a singular verdict, not a process, but genuine saving faith is the kind that perseveres.

— desiringgod.org/messages/the-purpose-and-perseverance-of-faith

### Reformed (Ligonier / Covenant Theology):

The Ligonier devotional calls Genesis 15 the chapter that "inaugurates God's covenant with Abraham." God's promise of seed connects to Genesis 3:15 (the seed of the woman) and points forward to Christ. God escorts Abram outside and gives a "fourfold reassurance" — shield, reward, offspring, land — "given in circumstances that to the outward eye disclose no basis for hope."

— learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-great-reward (accessed via search excerpt)

On the covenant ceremony (vv. 17–21), Ligonier interprets the self-maledictory oath as God saying: "So may it be done to me and mine, if I fail to fulfill this promise to you." The divided animals are "prophetic of what redemption would in fact cost: the severing of Jesus from the embrace of His Father in heaven" (Isaiah 53:8, Zechariah 13:7). Christ took the curse so believers receive Abraham's blessing (Galatians 3:13–14).

— learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-great-reward (search excerpt)

### Lutheran (Luther, cited in Enduring Word):

"When the article of justification has fallen, everything has fallen…. This is the chief article from which all other doctrines have flowed…. It alone begets, nourishes, builds, preserves, and defends the church of God; and without it the church of God cannot exist for one hour."

— Luther, cited by Boice, at enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

### On the "New Perspective on Paul" (modern scholarly debate):

The search for N.T. Wright / new perspective material on Genesis 15:6 did not return usable results within the allowed sites. This is a known scholarly debate — whether "righteousness" here means imputed forensic righteousness (traditional Reformation) or covenant membership / covenant faithfulness — but no accessible page was retrieved from the permitted domains.

## vv. 7–8 — "I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur… to give you this land." / "Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?"

**Traditional reading:**

God restates the land promise with a preface that anchors it in His identity: "I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur." Abram's question — "how shall I know?" — seems surprising after v. 6, but it reflects a common experience: faith can waver moments after it is exercised. Spurgeon is quoted: "What! Abraham, is not God's promise sufficient for thee?… Ah, beloved! faith is often marred by a measure of unbelief."

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Gill defends Abram: he was not doubting but asking for further confirmation, like Gideon (Judges 6:36) and Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:8) — good men who asked for signs without blame. Even Ahaz was blamed for *not* asking one (Isaiah 7:10).

— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/15.htm

Ellicott agrees: Abram asked "not from want of faith, but from a desire for a more direct confirmation of the promise and fuller knowledge of the details."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

Abram had "no title deed to the land, no certificate of ownership." All he had was God's promise.

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

---

## vv. 9–11 — The animals: heifer, goat, ram (each three years old), turtledove, young pigeon; cut in half; birds of prey driven away.

**Traditional reading:**

God tells Abram to prepare a covenant ceremony. The cutting of animals was a known ANE practice for treaty-making (cf. Jeremiah 34:18–20). The parties would walk between the halves, essentially saying: "May the same happen to me if I break this covenant." The Hebrew for "made a covenant" (v. 18) is literally "cut a covenant" (*karath berith*).

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Ellicott: The three-year-old animals were at full maturity. The birds were not divided — there were two, so Abram likely placed one on each side. Birds of prey descending represents "enemies of Israel" who would try to devour them. Abram driving them away signifies prayer and faith protecting the covenant.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

Gill adds extensive rabbinic speculation: some Jewish interpreters saw the animals as representing the four world monarchies (Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome), while the undivided birds represented Israel preserved through affliction.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/15.htm

---

## vv. 12–16 — Deep sleep, terror, darkness; prophecy of 400 years of slavery, judgment on the oppressor, return in the fourth generation; Abram's peaceful death.

**Traditional reading:**

At sunset, God caused a "deep sleep" (*tardemah*) to fall on Abram — the same word used of Adam (Genesis 2:21). Terror and great darkness accompanied divine manifestation (cf. Job 4:12–16; Daniel 10:8).

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

The 400 years of affliction refers to Israel's slavery in Egypt. Ellicott notes the exact sojourn was 430 years (Exodus 12:40–41). The "fourth generation" (v. 16) corresponds to the four centuries — an indication of long human lifespans in the patriarchal era. The word *dor* (generation) may have signified roughly a century in ancient usage.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

The Amorites are named as representative of all the Canaanite nations. The delay in Israel's possession of the land is explained: "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete." God would not dispossess them until their sin had reached its full measure — a principle of divine justice. The conquest of Canaan was "not by any wilful decree to make room for Israel, but as an act of justice."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

"You, however, will go to your fathers in peace" (v. 15): Ellicott says this phrase, used here for the first time, "evidently involves the thought of the immortality of the soul. The body may be buried far away, but the soul joins the company of its forefathers in some separate abode."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

---

## vv. 17–21 — The smoking firepot and flaming torch pass between the pieces; the covenant is made; the land boundaries are given.

**Traditional reading:**

God alone — represented by the "smoking oven" (or firepot) and "burning torch" — passed between the animal halves while Abram watched passively. This makes it a **unilateral covenant**: God signed for both parties. The certainty rests on God's character, not Abram's performance. "Abram could not break a contract he never signed!"

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Ellicott notes the "smoking furnace" is the circular firepot used for warmth. Fire is the "recognised symbol of the Deity" (burning bush, pillar of fire, Sinai lightning). Two emblems — smoke and fire — but one divine presence passing through. Abram probably also passed between the pieces earlier in the day, and now Jehovah does the same.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

The land boundaries span "from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates." Under Solomon (1 Kings 8:65) and possibly Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), Israel briefly controlled this territory as a token of permanent future possession.

— enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-15/

Ellicott clarifies: "the river of Egypt" here (Hebrew *nahar*) means the Nile itself — a constantly flowing river, distinct from the Wadi el-Arish (the "torrent of Egypt"). Abram's descendants are promised a kingdom "conterminous with the Nile and the Euphrates." However, the ten named nations limit the grant to their specific territories.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

The list of ten nations (vv. 19–21): Ellicott identifies the Kenites as an Arab race friendly to Israel (including Jethro); the Kenizzites as the clan of Caleb (Numbers 32:12); the Kadmonites as an otherwise unknown eastern or ancient people. The rest — Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaites, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, Jebusites — are the familiar Canaanite peoples.

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/15.htm

**Reformed covenant reading (Ligonier):**

The self-maledictory oath was "God's way of saying, 'So may it be done to me and mine, if I fail to fulfill this promise to you.'" The divided animals prefigure Christ being "cut off" (Isaiah 53:8), the Father's drawn sword against the Son (Zechariah 13:7), so that believers receive the Abrahamic blessing (Galatians 3:13–14). God "did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32) as he will Abraham's son, Isaac (Genesis 22:12)."

— learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-great-reward (search excerpt)

**Regarding the Abrahamic covenant today (Reformed view from Ligonier):**

The Abrahamic covenant "is still in operation in the sense that it has been fulfilled" — the promise is realized in Christ. Paul says in Galatians 3:13–14 that Christ became a curse so the Abrahamic blessings could come to the Gentiles. There are not two tracks of salvation (one for physical Israel, one for the church). Christ fulfills the covenant.

— learn.ligonier.org/qas/is-the-abrahamic-covenant-still-operative-today (search excerpt)

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Emphases

| Issue | Baptist / Reformed (Piper, Desiring God) | Classic Reformed (Ligonier) | Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word) |
|-------|------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| v. 6 Righteousness | Faith unites to Christ; His alien righteousness is imputed | Same; covenant context emphasized | Salvation by grace through faith; personal trust in God's promise |
| Covenant in vv. 17-18 | Unilateral, God's character alone secures it | Self-maledictory oath; Christological typology in divided animals | Unilateral; God cannot fail; believers "merely enter by faith" |
| Land promise | Fulfilled in Christ; spiritual seed includes Gentiles | Fulfilled in Christ; one covenant people | Literal future possession for Israel as well as spiritual fulfilment |
